records.description: Mossbauer transmission spectra record gamma attenuation as relative source/absorber velocity is varied. A fitted center shift, quadrupole splitting, linewidth and relative spectral area are inferred spectral parameters, distinct from a directly observed atomic geometry, absolute recoilless fraction or complete vibrational density of states. In the selected harmonic displacement convention, write f=exp(-k_gamma^2*mean(u_parallel^2)), where u_parallel is displacement projected along the gamma wave vector. In the selected Debye analysis, center shift contains isomer and second-order-Doppler contributions, while normalized thin-absorber area probes relative f. These two routes need not yield one identical effective Debye temperature.

contexts.finding: The selected dried Fe-gluconate specimen has a broad XRD pattern classified as amorphous, in contrast with the crystalline hydrated parent specimen. Fe-57 velocity-dependent transmission spectra show resonant attenuation at finite absorber temperatures across the reported 78-295 K study; Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. This is a positive bound-solid Mossbauer case whose absorber is not reported to possess perfect periodic crystal order. The three-doublet analysis yields finite widths and distinct center shifts and quadrupole splittings under the stated spectral model. At 295 K its normalized area quantities a1,a2,a3 are 0.49,0.46,0.52 relative to 78 K. The model-derived effective Debye temperatures differ: Table 2 reports 377(9) K from CS1 and 204(4) K from a1. These results illustrate finite-temperature spectral and vibrational sensitivity, with fitted hyperfine/electronic-environment interpretation, rather than a natural-width measurement or absolute recoilless probability.
limitations: This is one primary experiment context containing sample X-ray characterization and finite-temperature transmission spectroscopy. Its spectra, fitted components, relative areas and Debye interpretations share the same specimen/measurements; they are not independent replications.

The measured sample is powdered Fe-gluconate prepared by dissolution and drying at 50 degrees C. XRD-amorphous is the reported finite-sensitivity diffraction classification, not proof that every atomic neighborhood has no order.

The source reports about 10 mg Fe per cm^2, 1024 channels, source at room temperature, 78-295 K absorber range and temperature stability within plus/minus 0.1 K. These preparation/control values are not error bars on fitted shifts or proof of the thin-absorber approximation for every material.

The quoted typical Table 1 errors are source estimates, without a reconstructed confidence convention or complete covariance/systematic budget. No raw counts, background, thickness correction, calibration fit or independent uncertainty replay was obtained.

The earlier crystalline comparison study and imported Debye/isomer-shift references are not separately reviewed or admitted as additional studies. The original 1959 paper was not obtained as actual article text; a seven-page anthology contents PDF is not that article.

The XRD classification and transmission profiles establish a finite observed case; they do not measure a universal ordering threshold, a unique local coordination geometry or an exactly absent crystalline volume fraction.
Figure 2 displays 78 K and 268 K examples. The study range reaches 295 K; the plotted higher-temperature example must not be relabelled 295 K.

The fitted D1,D2,D3 curves are model components overlaid on measured spectra. Their existence as a useful decomposition does not alone establish three unique phases, three distinct atom positions or an independent magnetic-ordering measurement.
The transmission scale is relative; no new absolute absorption cross section, absolute gamma-emission probability, natural linewidth or independent f measurement is inferred.

Table 1 center shifts are relative to the Co-57/Rh source at room temperature, not automatically to metallic alpha-Fe. Its shift, splitting and full-width-at-half-maximum entries are in mm/s; the fitted widths are not natural nuclear energy widths.

At 295 K the table lists a1,a2,a3 as 0.49,0.46,0.52 after normalization to unity at 78 K. These are relative normalized spectral-area quantities under the stated approximation, not absolute probabilities f(295 K).

The text writes a_k=(A_k/B)/a_k(78 K), with B the background counts. This notation reuses a_k on the normalization reference; retain the stated background and 78 K normalization without claiming a new independent absolute normalization or repaired raw-data definition.

Three-doublet fitting associates D1,D2 with Fe(II) and D3 with Fe(III) from their spectral parameters. Relative component areas are not automatically atom-number fractions when component recoilless fractions differ; no new exact Fe(III) population or unique geometry is admitted.

The source Table 1 nominal area row at 268 K sums to 101.0 percent, so its rounded fitted entries are not promoted to an exact probability-normalized mixture. No correction or recalculated row is invented.

Table 2 gives effective Debye temperatures 377(9) K from CS1 and 204(4) K from a1. Parenthesized errors retain the source convention, without an invented confidence level or full shared-data covariance. The two routes are different weightings/assumptions, not independent proof of one exact Debye temperature.

The page 7 prose refers to Table 3 for these values although the adjacent displayed table is Table 2. This is a source cross-reference discrepancy, not an additional unseen table or a reason to silently renumber the source.

limitations: PNP detects the ion after coherent radial-to-axial transfer. Its resonant voltages differ for N+ and N2+, changing equilibrium position in stray fields. The SOF protocol keeps the evolution voltage common and changes it only for detection.

The SOF signal is a classical cyclotron amplitude produced by two separated pulses, not a quantum-state amplitude or an entanglement measurement. Figure 1 uses evolution times up to 50 s for the precision estimate.

Figure 2 compares an N+ ion at approximately 5 V with the same species at 10 V and an N2+ ion at 10 V, with a 22.5 mV axial offset. The approximately 3 ppb unequal-voltage shift disappears at the reported precision with the common-voltage procedure.

Table I bounds residual magnetic, electrostatic and relativistic systematic terms at approximately 0.030, 0.025 and 0.020 ppb for the specified N+/N2+ settings. These are configuration-specific error estimates, not zero corrections or universal bounds.

The first two Table II(a) reference ratios depend on electron mass and binding energies. Their agreement near 0.15 ppb tests those controls; it does not prove absence of every systematic effect in all other ion comparisons.
The measured ion has three trap modes. The free cyclotron frequency is reconstructed from their squared frequencies; the trap cyclotron mode alone is not the free frequency.
The paper writes omega_c=q*B/(m*c) in Gaussian units. In SI the expression is omega_c=abs(q)*B/m for the frequency magnitude; an angular frequency differs from cycles per second by 2*pi.

For the same magnetic field, omega_2/omega_1=(m_1/abs(q_1))/(m_2/abs(q_2)). Equal charges permit a mass ratio; the Ar+/Ar++ entry requires the charge factor and is not a literal ratio of almost equal ionic masses.
The ions are loaded and measured alternately, not simultaneously. Removing a fitted magnetic drift does not make all residuals or adjacent ratios statistically independent.
These are reported measurements and conditional inferences. Raw phase records, drift fits, chemical-energy inputs and complete covariance have not been independently replayed.

A charged-ion frequency, neutral-atom mass and inferred neutron mass are different quantities. These results do not establish nucleon formation, lifetime, stability or a universal constituent minimum.

The 1993 and 1994 publications belong to the same MIT measurement program. Disjoint acquisition and cross-publication covariance are not established; the two papers cannot be treated as independent replications or averaged as independent results.

limitations: The carbon-12 neutral-atom reference has mass exactly 12 u by definition. A carbon ion differs by electron mass and ionization energy; treating C+ as exactly 12 u is incorrect.

Converting molecular-ion comparisons to neutral isolated ground-state atoms requires electron, chemical-binding and ionization-energy terms. The 1994 analysis uses ideal-gas heats of formation at 0 K; this is not the trap temperature.
A neutral hydrogen atom is not a bare proton and a neutral deuterium atom is not a deuteron. Nuclear masses require removal of electronic contributions.
Table II(b) of the 1993 paper expresses masses in nu (1e-9 u). Its H and D values become 1.0078250317(7) u and 2.0141017779(6) u; the 1994 H value is 1.0078250316(5) u.

limitations: PNP detects the ion after coherent radial-to-axial transfer. Its resonant voltages differ for N+ and N2+, changing equilibrium position in stray fields. The SOF protocol keeps the evolution voltage common and changes it only for detection.

The SOF signal is a classical cyclotron amplitude produced by two separated pulses, not a quantum-state amplitude or an entanglement measurement. Figure 1 uses evolution times up to 50 s for the precision estimate.

Figure 2 compares an N+ ion at approximately 5 V with the same species at 10 V and an N2+ ion at 10 V, with a 22.5 mV axial offset. The approximately 3 ppb unequal-voltage shift disappears at the reported precision with the common-voltage procedure.

Table I bounds residual magnetic, electrostatic and relativistic systematic terms at approximately 0.030, 0.025 and 0.020 ppb for the specified N+/N2+ settings. These are configuration-specific error estimates, not zero corrections or universal bounds.

The first two Table II(a) reference ratios depend on electron mass and binding energies. Their agreement near 0.15 ppb tests those controls; it does not prove absence of every systematic effect in all other ion comparisons.
The measured ion has three trap modes. The free cyclotron frequency is reconstructed from their squared frequencies; the trap cyclotron mode alone is not the free frequency.
The paper writes omega_c=q*B/(m*c) in Gaussian units. In SI the expression is omega_c=abs(q)*B/m for the frequency magnitude; an angular frequency differs from cycles per second by 2*pi.

For the same magnetic field, omega_2/omega_1=(m_1/abs(q_1))/(m_2/abs(q_2)). Equal charges permit a mass ratio; the Ar+/Ar++ entry requires the charge factor and is not a literal ratio of almost equal ionic masses.
The ions are loaded and measured alternately, not simultaneously. Removing a fitted magnetic drift does not make all residuals or adjacent ratios statistically independent.
These are reported measurements and conditional inferences. Raw phase records, drift fits, chemical-energy inputs and complete covariance have not been independently replayed.

A charged-ion frequency, neutral-atom mass and inferred neutron mass are different quantities. These results do not establish nucleon formation, lifetime, stability or a universal constituent minimum.

The 1993 and 1994 publications belong to the same MIT measurement program. Disjoint acquisition and cross-publication covariance are not established; the two papers cannot be treated as independent replications or averaged as independent results.
